{{Short description|Method in Itô calculus}}
{{dablink|This article is about numerical methods in stochastic models ([[stochastic differential equation]]s). For the same problem but for deterministic models see [[Euler method]] and [[Ordinary differential equation]].}}

In [[Itô calculus]], the '''Euler–Maruyama method''' (also simply called the '''Euler method''') is a method for the approximate [[numerical analysis|numerical solution]] of a [[stochastic differential equation]] (SDE). It is an extension of the [[Euler method]] for [[ordinary differential equation]]s to stochastic differential equations named after [[Leonhard Euler]] and [[Gisiro Maruyama]]. The same generalization cannot be done for any arbitrary deterministic method.<ref>{{cite book|author1-link=Peter Kloeden|author2-link=Eckhard Platen |author1=Kloeden, P.E. |author2= Platen, E. |name-list-style=amp | title=Numerical Solution of Stochastic Differential Equations | publisher=Springer, Berlin | year=1992 | isbn=3-540-54062-8 }}</ref>

==Definition==

Consider the stochastic differential equation (see [[Itô calculus]])

:<math>\mathrm{d} X_t = a(X_t, t) \, \mathrm{d} t + b(X_t, t) \, \mathrm{d} W_t,</math>

with [[initial condition]] ''X''<sub>0</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''<sub>0</sub>, where ''W''<sub>''t''</sub> denotes the [[Wiener process]], and suppose that we wish to solve this SDE on some interval of time [0,&nbsp;''T'']. Then the '''Euler–Maruyama approximation''' to the true solution ''X'' is the [[Markov chain]] ''Y'' defined as follows:

* Partition the interval [0,&nbsp;''T''] into ''N'' equal subintervals of width <math>\Delta t>0</math>:

::<math>0 = \tau_{0} < \tau_{1} < \cdots < \tau_{N} = T \text{ and } \Delta t = T/N;</math>

* Set ''Y''<sub>0</sub>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''<sub>0</sub>
* Recursively define ''Y''<sub>''n''</sub> for 0&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''n''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''N-1'' by

::<math>\, Y_{n + 1} = Y_n + a(Y_n, \tau_n) \, \Delta t + b(Y_n, \tau_n) \, \Delta W_n,</math>

:where

::<math>\Delta W_n = W_{\tau_{n + 1}} - W_{\tau_n}.</math>

The [[random variable]]s Δ''W''<sub>''n''</sub> are [[independent and identically distributed]] [[normal distribution|normal random variables]] with [[expected value]] zero and [[variance]] Δ''t''.

===Derivation===

The Euler-Maruyama formula can be derived by considering the integral form of the Itô SDE

:<math>X_{\tau_{n+1}} = X_{\tau_n} + \int_{\tau_n}^{\tau_{n+1}} a(X_s, s) \, ds + \int_{\tau_n}^{\tau_{n+1}} b(X_s, s) \, dW_s</math>

and approximating <math>a(X_s, s) \approx a(X_n, \tau_n)</math> and <math>b(X_s, s) \approx b(X_n, \tau_n)</math> on the small time interval <math>[\tau_n, \tau_{n+1}]</math>.

==Strong and weak convergence==

Like other approximation methods, the accuracy of the Euler–Maruyama scheme is analyzed through comparison to an underlying continuous solution.
Let <math>X</math> denote an Itô process over <math>[0,T]</math>, equal to

:<math>
X_t = X_0 + \int_0^t \mu(s, X_s) ds + \int_0^t \sigma(s, X_s) dW_s
</math>

at time <math>t \in [0,T]</math>, where <math>\mu</math> and <math>\sigma</math> denote deterministic "drift" and "diffusion" functions, respectively, and <math>W_t</math> is the [[Wiener process]].
As discrete approximations of continuous processes are typically assessed through comparison between their respective final states at <math>T>0</math>, a natural convergence criterion for such discrete processes is

:<math>
\lim_{N \to \infty} \mathbb{E} \left[ \left| \hat{X}_N - X_T \right| \right] = 0.
</math>

Here, <math>\hat{X}_N</math> corresponds to the final state of the discrete process <math>\hat{X}</math>, which approximates <math>X_T</math> by taking <math>N</math> steps of length <math>\Delta t = T/N</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | last = Higham
 | first = Desmond J.
 | title = An Algorithmic Introduction to Numerical Simulation of Stochastic Differential Equations
 | journal = SIAM Review
 | volume = 43
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 525–546
 | publisher = Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics
 | year = 2001
 | issn = 0036-1445
 | location = Philadelphia, PA
}}</ref>
Iterative schemes satisfying the above condition are said to strongly converge to the continuous process <math>X</math>, which automatically implies their satisfaction of the weak convergence criterion,

:<math>
\lim_{N \to \infty}\left| \mathbb{E} \left[  g(\hat{X}_N)\right] - \left[ g(X_T)  \right] \right| = 0,
</math>

for any bounded and continuous function <math>g</math>.
<ref>{{cite book |author1=Kloeden, P.E. |author2= Platen, E. |name-list-style=amp | title=Numerical Solution of Stochastic Differential Equations | publisher=Springer, Berlin | year=1992 | isbn=3-540-54062-8 }}</ref>
More specifically, if there exists a constant <math>K</math> and <math>\gamma_s, \delta_0 > 0</math> such that

:<math>
\mathbb{E} \left[ \left| \hat{X}_N - X_T \right| \right] \leq K \delta_0^{\gamma_s}
</math>

for any <math>\delta \in (0,\delta_0)</math>, the approximation converges strongly with order <math>\gamma_s</math> to the continuous process <math>X</math>; 
likewise, <math>\hat{X}</math> converges weakly to <math>X</math> with order <math>\gamma_w</math> if the same inequality holds for the expectation of <math>g(\hat{X}_N) - g(X_T) </math>.
Strong order <math>\gamma_s</math> convergence implies weak order <math>\gamma_w \geq \gamma_s</math> convergence:
exemplifying this, it was shown in 1972<ref>{{Cite book
 | last1 = Gikhman
 | first1 = Iosif I.
 | last2 = Skorokhod
 | first2 = Anatoli V.
 | last3 = Kotz
 | first3 = S.
 | title = The Theory of Stochastic Processes III
 | series = Classics in Mathematics
 | edition = 1
 | publisher = Springer Berlin / Heidelberg
 | year = 2007
 | location = Berlin, Heidelberg
 | isbn = 9783540499404
 | language = en
}}</ref>
that the Euler–Maruyama method strongly converges with order <math>\gamma_s = 1/2</math> to any Itô process, provided <math>\mu, \sigma</math> satisfy Lipschitz continuity and linear growth conditions with respect to <math>x</math>, and in 1974, the Euler–Maruyama scheme was proven to converge weakly with order <math>\gamma_w = 1</math> to Itô processes governed by the same such <math>\mu, \sigma</math>,<ref>{{Cite journal
 | last = Mil’shtein
 | first = G. N.
 | title = A Method of Second-Order Accuracy Integration of Stochastic Differential Equations
 | journal = Theory of Probability and Its Applications
 | volume = 23
 | issue = 2
 | pages = 396–401
 | publisher = Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics
 | year = 1979
 | issn = 0040-585X
 | location = Philadelphia
}}</ref>
provided that their derivatives also satisfy similar conditions.<ref>{{Cite journal
 | last = Mil’shtejn
 | first = G. N.
 | title = Approximate Integration of Stochastic Differential Equations
 | journal = Theory of Probability and Its Applications
 | volume = 19
 | issue = 3
 | pages = 557–562
 | publisher = Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics
 | year = 1975
 | issn = 0040-585X
 | location = Philadelphia
}}</ref>

==Example with geometric Brownian motion==
[[Image:GBM simulation.png|right|thumb|500px|Simulation of geometric Brownian motion. Solid lines show an analytic solution, dashed lines show the Euler-Maruyama method.]]
[[File:EM strong convergence.png|thumb|Strong error convergence plot for Euler-Maruyama.]]
[[File:EM weak convergence.png|thumb|Weak error convergence plot for Euler-Maruyama.]]

A simple case to analyze is [[geometric Brownian motion]], which satisfies the SDE

:<math>dX_t = \lambda X_t\,dt + \sigma X_t\,dW_t</math>

for fixed <math>\lambda</math> and <math>\sigma</math>.  
Applying [[Itô lemma|Itô’s lemma]] to <math>\ln X_t</math> yields the closed-form solution  

:<math>
X_t = X_0 \exp\left( \left(\lambda - \tfrac{1}{2} \sigma^2\right)t + \sigma W_t \right)
</math>

Discretising with Euler–Maruyama gives the time-step updates

:<math>
Y_{n+1} = \left(1 + \lambda\Delta t + \sigma\Delta W_n\right) Y_n = Y_0 \prod_{k=0}^{n} \left(1 + \lambda\Delta t + \sigma\Delta W_k\right)
</math>

By using a [[Taylor series]] expansion of the exponential function in the analytic solution, we can get a formula for the exact update in a time-step.

:<math>
\begin{align}
X_{\tau_{k+1}} &= X_{\tau_k} \exp\left( (\lambda - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\Delta t + \sigma\Delta W_k \right) \\
& = X_{\tau_k}\left[ 1 + \lambda\Delta t + \sigma\Delta W_k + \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2\left((\Delta W_k)^2 - \Delta t\right) + O\left(\Delta t^{3/2}\right) \right] \\
\end{align}
</math>

Summing the local errors between the analytic and Euler-Maruyama solutions over each of the <math>N = T / \Delta t</math> steps gives the strong error estimate

:<math>
\mathbb{E}\left[\,|X_T - Y_N|\,\right] = O\left(\sqrt{\Delta t}\right)
</math>

confirming strong order <math>1/2</math> convergence.

Another numerical aspect to consider is stability. The path's second moment is  
<math>
\mathbb{E}|X_t|^2 \propto \exp\left((2\lambda + \sigma^2)t\right)
</math>,  
so long-time decay of the solution occurs only when <math>2\lambda + \sigma^2 < 0</math>.  
The Euler–Maruyama scheme preserves variance decay in this case provided that  
<math>
\Delta t \leq \frac{-1}{\lambda^2}\left(2\lambda + \sigma^2\right)
</math>.

==Application==

[[File:Equação Diferencial Estocástica.jpg|thumbnail|[[Gene expression]] modelled as a stochastic process.]]

An area that has benefited significantly from SDEs is [[mathematical biology]]. As many biological processes are both stochastic and continuous in nature, numerical methods of solving SDEs are highly valuable in the field.
